name: ADHD Support
description: Support for attention regulation, task initiation, focus management, and organisation that many people with ADHD find helpful.

immediateActions.title: Focus Timer Sprint
instructions: Choose ONE single task you want to work on right now
Write the task down so it is visible: I will work on [task] for 15 minutes
Set a timer for 15 minutes
Remove obvious distractions: put phone in another room, close extra tabs
Work only on that task until the timer rings
When the timer ends, stand up, stretch, and decide: 5-minute break or another sprint?

immediateActions.title: Task Breakdown: First 3 Steps
instructions: Write down the project or task that feels overwhelming
Ask yourself: What is the very first physical action I could take? (e.g. open document, get pen)
Write Step 1 in one line
Ask: If I finished Step 1, what would Step 2 be?
Write Step 2 and Step 3 the same way
Put your list somewhere visible and start Step 1 right now

immediateActions.title: Pomodoro with Sensory Reset
instructions: Set a timer for 25 minutes of focused work on one task
During work: if distractions pop into your head, write them on a notepad to return to later
When the 25 minutes end, write down exactly where you stopped so you can resume easily
Take a 5-minute sensory reset break: stand up, walk around, drink water, look away from the screen
After the break, do a quick 3-2-1 countdown and resume where you left off

immediateActions.title: Priority Planning Matrix
instructions: List all the tasks currently on your mind
Circle the top 3 that have real deadlines or consequences today
From those 3, pick the ONE that gives you the most anxiety or relief when finished
Estimate how long each circled task will take
Schedule the hardest task at your personal best time of day
Cross everything else off today's list; it can wait

safetyGuidance: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental difference with many strengths, and there are effective strategies and supports available. If ADHD symptoms are significantly affecting your work, relationships, or quality of life, consider speaking with a healthcare provider or mental health professional who specialises in ADHD. Remember to be patient and kind to yourself as you find what works best for you.
